[2024-03-06 11:42] poletz : some premises: i considered just the top 3 leagues (so 7 conferences total)  i considered just the top 3 teams of each of those conferences i considered just the two most potg of those teams (in case of more than 2, i considered the best +/- among them) i considered just conference stats calculated player efficiency: EFF=(PTS + REB + AST + STL + BLK − Missed FG − Missed FT - TO)  calculated adjusted efficiency that is Em=(EFF/min played) x 40  then adjusted it aslo for team avg possessions so the final values is Adj EFF= (Em/pos) x 100  ADJUSTED EFFICIENCY IS THE COEFFICIENT THAT SAYS HOW MUCH A PLAYER HAS BEEN EFFICIENT COMPARING THEM ON THE SAME POSS AND MIN PLAYED then i missed a coefficient to evaluate defence (even if steals and blocks are already on it) so i took inverted OeFG halved by2 (es Oefg: 40% -> def coeff: (60/2=30). so the final INDEX (need to find a proper name) is the sum of ADJ EFF + DEF COEF

[2024-04-10 17:30] fatherborf : i feel like i may have asked this before but how does RPI quite work? i had a high of .577 then lost a game and fell to .566, won 4 in a row since by an avg of 31.75ppg, now its down to .560
[2024-04-10 17:30] fatherborf : oh, .561 now, so went up 0.001 after todays win, but fell after each of the 3 wins before
[2024-04-10 17:30] eljefe7705 : RPI is calculated from the team's winning percentage (WP), the opponents' winning percentage (OWP) and the opponents' opponents' winning percentage (OOWP). These three components are combined to produce the RPI using the following formula: RPI = (WP * WPVAL) + (OWP * OWPVAL) + (OOWP * OOWPVAL).
[2024-04-10 17:31] fatherborf : ahh okay so OWP and OOWP i did not realize were quite such big factors
[2024-04-10 17:31] eljefe7705 : In its current formulation, the index comprises a team's winning percentage (25%), its opponents' winning percentage (50%), and the winning percentage of those opponents' opponents (25%). The opponents' winning percentage and the winning percentage of those opponents' opponents both comprise the strength of schedule (SOS). Thus, the SOS accounts for 75% of the RPI calculation and is 2/3 its opponents' winning percentage and 1/3 its opponents' opponents' winning percentages.
[2024-04-10 17:32] fatherborf : that makes sense, my SOS has fallen from like .510 to .488
[2024-04-10 17:32] eljefe7705 : so if you're in a lower division/league, most conference games will lower your RPI due to lowering SOS

[2024-04-26 19:52] poletz : <@799707004335292467> i answer here in order to not spam the poll channel. my intent was to create a system to identify the best players for each role in the most analytical way possible.  the criteria are: role is the preferred role in roster page. and they need to ve played at least 600 mins in conf games (only those are considered) so there are 4 criteria: -true shooting % (=shooting efficiency) -adjusted points (=shooting volume : points scored adjusted by minutes played and team possessions) -adjusted bonus (=gameplay volume: (As+St+Bl+Re+Fd-Pf-To) adjusted by minutes played and team possessions) -ofg% (=defensive effciency) for each of those categories each players get a rank (from 1 to N players eligible) -> i show it on a % (I.E. 9TH/275 = 3,3%.. he is in the best 3,3% for this category)  then sum all this points and the list them from the lower one (that is the best) to the higher (that is the worst) all the rest are just additional infos about team, level, league position and players stas.

[2024-05-03 15:41] infinite_tea : Thanks for the shout-out, <@711316787471581294>! My first podcast mention (since I wasn't playing during the time the podcast was active).  To answer your question, Booker was a headache for me all year... I tried to get him to shoot more, but he was already shooting 32% with 2-3 3s per game, so when he shot more, that percentage just got worse. He just seemed like an unreliable scoring option, so I leaned on his driving/speed instead. And I think Levy's stats are a bit misleading. I played in a conference where Cs were very weak, so I had him set as our primary option during most of the conference play and he dominated. But whenever he played dominant defensive Cs, he disappeared and cost me games. So in the tournament, I leaned away from him (and into a drive/dish type offense) and I think that's why I was able to make it so far. I'm big on efficient scoring, rather than volume.

[2024-05-20 03:09] _plokmijn : Used my player ratings sheet to create a similar breakdown. Differs quite a bit from my original II.2 prediction in the forums since I realized there were a couple issues in the rating system. Players are rated based on height and skills relevant to their position. 70 is considered an average skilled player for that position. SFs tend to be a bit underrated since it is hard to capture all of the different archetypes that make a good SF. Good bigs also get rated very highly since there are fewer skills that set them apart from an "average" big. PI = Plok Index, WPI = Weighted Plok Index which is a 3:1 weighted average of starters to bench PI. A lot of teams I only added a 3 man bench since those players play a majority of the bench minutes.

[2024-05-23 10:34] _plokmijn : Each player is assigned a rating based on their skills and height relative to each position. 70 is considered average, so a player above 70 is an above average player at that position and under 70 is a below average player for that position. I sifted through each teams depth charts to figure out which position players are being primarily used at, and then inputted them into the table to rank against the rest of the conference.
[2024-05-23 10:37] _plokmijn : The idea is to determine how good a player is based on their skills/height for their position, and not rely on SI since guards and bigs have a decent gap in average SI

[2024-06-24 18:52] gards710 : a couple of things: redshirting ANY player causes a penalty in recruiting, it is just that redshirting 1-3 star players has a minimal effect that is outweighed by things like graduating players, time passing, etc. But you may notice at some points once you play for a bit that recruiting players in a demographic that once was super easy all of a sudden becomes more difficult. That is likely due to redshirting everyone and probably a bit of a logjam at a certain position.  The penalty affects recruits of all levels.  The penalty will happen whenever you RS a player, no matter if they are a FR or not. But it theoretically hurts more when they are a FR because recruits see the redshirt AND a younger player, whereas if you RS them as a JR for instance, it is an older player (and thus would not be competition for playing time)

"However, two more curveballs came in the form of game changing updates announced by Steve that would usher in the 2021 and 2022 seasons. One change was a limit on the number of players that could be offensively positioned in the paint with an automatic repositioning farther out. This was done to more realistically consider the amount of room available in the paint but also restrain the "all bigs" tactics -- which many felt was a bit overpowering. This became known as the “NYU Rule.” Additionally, the game engine was altered to increase 3-point opportunities to be more in-line with today’s college game. Suddenly, size, which had been such a strategic advantage in the beginning and whose impacts had been slowly scaled back since then, was delivered another significant blow, while 3-pt shooting which was so bonkers in the beginning was the recipient of new relevance"

[2024-08-30 15:10] flushednevada : It’s a tough question to answer - I’ve seen presidents suggest that the type of defense you run can directly impact it. So more pressure or man defense would result in more fouls vs zone. I believe that IQ plays a role, since it modifies outcomes - a smart player is less likely to foul, in the same way that a smart player is less likely to take a bad shot. But my claims are purely anecdotal, I can’t back it up with anything definitive.  It also logically follows that, if your team plays at a slower pace your players may foul out less frequently due to a reduction in opportunity.

[2024-09-30 23:15] fatherborf : Yep, good advice. Kind of to what you want as a manager, but my personal thing is I usually leave it at Any and only do Up if I am basically 100% sure I will be nabbing a tourney invite regardless, so having better non-conf can help the RPI for a better seed.  But if you're gonna struggle to survive, it can be risky, as conference games count much more for tourney purposes, but it's still not necessarily easy to climb out of a 2-8 start or something. Down is good for win total but IMO once you are LL4 or even LL5, winning by a bunch against teams 20-30+ WSI lower than you can make it hard to know how your team actually performs against even competition, and ironically can also hurt RPI - SOS is a factor and if your first ten opponents combine to go 10-90 you get the season Bates started 10-0 but also had the *lowest RPI in all of hardwood* going into conference games. that's technically another hole you now have to climb out of 😅
[2024-09-30 23:19] eljefe7705 : Down = easiest Any = usually harder Up = usually hardest  Depends what you want to do with your team. If you want to learn and test yourself/knowledge and see how good teams are structured, schedule Up  If you want to win at the risk of not learning as much about your team, schedule down  If you don't give a shit, schedule Any
[2024-09-30 23:22] eljefe7705 : When you're in D1, you generally want to follow these guidelines if you want to make the tourney: - League Level IV: always Schedule Up since your conference will probably not be great and conference play will drag your RPI down  - League Level III: probably still Up, but LL3 these days is better than it used to be so you could get away with Any  - League Level II: you will probably be in a tough conference, so Any or Down  - Legends (League Level I): the conference season will suck the soul right out of you, so schedule down

Denney quickly established himself by hitting into back to back to back to back shots from the inside as well as splashing 6 free throws early.   Denney's performance culminated in 24pts and 9 rebounds in 33 minutes of play and a 1 point win over the Trailblazers leading the charge to keep NC State's hopes for promotion alive.  Kudos and hats off to an incredible performance by the redshirt big man Mike Denney.

[2024-10-14 11:14] naph7777 : I think my own journey has been something like 1) SI Matters - I overprioritised SI, not even really caring that much about where the SI was. Skill were skills and I'd use them all. Didn't care enough about height, potential. Forever trying to compete with a (hopefully skilled) 6' 6" PF and a 6' 8" C. 2) Potential matters - I overprioritised potential, especially on guys with too low SI, hoping potential would make the difference 3) Height (and other physical attributes) matters - I wanted to be big almost everywhere and eventually swung too far and sacrificed too much SI & potential. 4) Build matters - I'm currently working my way through this, I'm probably at the point where a recruit's theoretical peak in various attributes isn't as important as what his actual peak will be with available playing time over the course of his career. ... X) Everything is in perfect balance and I can use my vast experience to select the best under-recruited recruits and dominate the HW universe.  I suspect I may not have enough personal SI, potential and time to reach X) 😛

[2024-11-12 00:08] fatherborf : yeah i would genuinely recommend practically ignoring fatigue and just do what you want. i had entire seasons without 4/5 of my starters getting a fatigue comment the entire season hoping to avoid injuries and it seems to unfortunately have no impact, or such a small impact as to be negligible. in general probably good to avoid it if youre competitive and need your defense at top notch the entire game, but like for RIT since i double fucked myself into a no hope season, took advantage of only having 10 players on scholarship and am RSing 5 while playing 5 and just running the 5 who are playing at 40 minutes a game to maximize all possible dev, and theyve started the season with less injuries than my minute managed, low pace, zone heavy style last season
[2024-11-12 00:31] fatherborf : as a track coach i would argue overuse and too much fatigue are the source of easily 90% of our injuries - a 2022 study for college track used a weirder unit of "1000 athletic exposures" which is defined to be any ncaa sanctioned practice or competition. so im not sure how it rates vs hours as practices are going to be longer than 1 hour, but most college trackletes are going to be running for only a small fraction of one total hour at a track meet, while also probably competing in multiple events - it found 3.99 for 1000 "athletic exposures"   two different drivers of injury create a positive feedback loop with overuse and excessively "going to the well" as the phrase we use a lot in track 1. the obvious one is that the # of chances of an injury to occur is going to increase the more a player is on the court/field/track, whatever. this part is straightforward, and with sports with actual human contact thats adding chances for stuff like hamstring pulls and stuff that happens due to contact with another person  2. is the less obvious one, but goes with the diminished performance: everyone can see the worse shots, slower movement, etc, but the the technique behind the fundamental movements of any sport or athletic activity are almost always not only centered around better performance, but also making more efficient movements and lowering injury risk to the player - the simple concepts of a RB or WR staying low in football while your stride and stature should be high and tall for top speed in a sprint as a perfect example - you will hit a marginally higher top speed running the latter way, but if you get hit running like that it might be the last time you ever even **can** run like that.
[2024-11-12 00:34] fatherborf : a tired lineman will position his feet and hands in ways that put more torque on their elbows and knees, a qb will throw more sloppily with accuracy but also in ways that direct more forces into muscles and tendons already tired. for basketball players, jumping into the air and then catching their giant frames gets less smooth, less efficient, etc. and its not going to necessarily be linear, it gets ugly fast. i think the fatigue misses this aspect of the performance decline, and at the very least there should be more of a compounding effect from back to back high fatigue games, especially if in-game theyre also with no rest between
[2024-11-12 00:37] fatherborf : and i say this as someone who is now more liberally putting players i like with absurd minutes. maybe some sort of compromise is in order where theres a bigger/any injury penalty to the fatigue, but maybe some modifier where if you play people a lot of minutes their stamina grows a little faster than it would otherwise? fair to argue its rational that if a guy with 5 stamina plays 25 games in a row at 35min/game hes probably gained some conditioning

[2024-11-26 22:55] aj22222. : What is the difference between shooting range and outside shot, same with inside and finishing?
[2024-11-26 23:48] naph7777 : IS is post play. Finishing is layups (close range shots on drives or in transition) I consider OS to be shooting form (how reliable & repeatable it is).  All shots are effected by range (closer shots easier, further shots harder), a high RNG attribute seems to reduce the penalty for long range shots (making them a better 3-point shooter for example)..... 3P% definitely seems to be effected by both OS and RNG, so its not as simple as OS = 2P jump shots and RNG = 3P jump shots.
